title: Loops and Iteration
subtitle: Loops and Iteration: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on loops and iteration, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Loops and Iteration: foundations and mental model

Loops and Iteration is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Loops need a clear stopping condition and progress toward it. Check empty, one-item, and boundary cases to catch infinite loops and off-by-one errors. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because A small lesson tracker can use tables and functions while keeping state changes and errors clear. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Loops and Iteration: Numeric for includes its end value
blocks.output: Numeric for includes its end value.

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “for lesson = 1, 4 do print(lesson) end”: Begins iteration over a numeric range or iterator. Expected behavior: Numeric for includes its end value. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A loop must print lesson numbers 1 through 10 exactly once. Which boundary rule includes lesson 10?
options: Start at 1 and continue while the counter is <= 10
Start at 1 and continue while the counter is < 1
Start at 0 and continue only while the counter is > 10
Increment the counter only when the loop finishes
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Start at 1 and continue while the counter is <= 10. The inclusive upper-bound test includes 10; the counter must advance every iteration.
blocks.reasoning: The inclusive upper-bound test includes 10; the counter must advance every iteration. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.question: A `while remaining > 0` loop never finishes. Which defect is most likely?
options: The output includes a newline
The variable has a descriptive name
The condition is evaluated before the body
The loop body never reduces or otherwise changes remaining toward the stop condition
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: The loop body never reduces or otherwise changes remaining toward the stop condition. A terminating loop must make progress toward a condition that eventually becomes false.
blocks.reasoning: A terminating loop must make progress toward a condition that eventually becomes false. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Loops and Iteration: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Loops need a clear stopping condition and progress toward it. Check empty, one-item, and boundary cases to catch infinite loops and off-by-one errors. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, A small lesson tracker can use tables and functions while keeping state changes and errors clear. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Loops and Iteration: Updates state so the loop will stop
blocks.code:
local remaining = 3
while remaining > 0 do print(remaining); remaining = remaining - 1 end
blocks.output: Updates state so the loop will stop.

blocks.text: Example 3 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “local remaining = 3”: Creates a local variable or table binding for this scope. Line 2 — “while remaining > 0 do print(remaining); remaining = remaining - 1 end”: Repeats the body while the condition remains true. Expected behavior: Updates state so the loop will stop. What if a line changes? If the loop update or stopping condition is removed or changed, iterations may be skipped, repeated, or never finish. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: An array has three elements. Which index-based condition avoids an out-of-range access?
options: i == array.length + 1
i < array.length
i <= array.length
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: i < array.length. The last valid index is length minus one, so the loop condition must stay strictly below length.
blocks.reasoning: The last valid index is length minus one, so the loop condition must stay strictly below length. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

Expected behavior: A condition limits which values are processed. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A loop should skip low scores but keep processing later scores. Which action fits?
options: Reset the index to zero
Continue the current iteration
Break out of the entire loop
Return from the whole function
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Continue the current iteration. Continue skips the current iteration, while break exits the loop.
blocks.reasoning: Continue skips the current iteration, while break exits the loop. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Loops and Iteration: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Loops need a clear stopping condition and progress toward it. Check empty, one-item, and boundary cases to catch infinite loops and off-by-one errors. For the Code Academy dashboard, A small lesson tracker can use tables and functions while keeping state changes and errors clear. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses loops and iteration. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A list can change size during iteration. What should the implementation do?
options: Use a deliberate iteration strategy and account for how changes affect indexes or iterators
Assume every index remains valid after any mutation
Ignore the collection’s size
Increment a counter without checking bounds
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Use a deliberate iteration strategy and account for how changes affect indexes or iterators. Mutating a collection can invalidate indexes or iterators and can cause missed or repeated items.
blocks.reasoning: Mutating a collection can invalidate indexes or iterators and can cause missed or repeated items. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
